title: Notification System: Complete Architecture
description: Design a multi-channel notification system with monolith and microservice architectures using React, ASP.NET Core, Azure, and AWS.

data.text: Design a multi-channel notification system like Firebase Cloud Messaging or Amazon SNS that can send email, SMS, push notifications (APNs/FCM), and in-app notifications to millions of users. The system must aggregate events to avoid spamming users, respect per-user channel preferences and quiet hours, support rich templates with variables, guarantee at-least-once delivery with deduplication, track delivery and engagement status, and handle 10 million notification sends per minute at peak load.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Send notifications across four channels: email (SendGrid/SES), SMS (Twilio/SNS), mobile push (APNs/FCM), and in-app (SignalR/WebSocket)
Template engine: admins create notification templates with variables (e.g. "Hi {{FirstName}}, your order {{OrderId}} shipped"), preview rendered output, and A/B test variants
Per-user channel preferences: users opt in/out of email, SMS, push per notification category (Order, Security, Marketing)
Quiet hours: suppress non-critical notifications during user-configured local time windows
Event aggregation and digest mode: batch 5 events within a 5-minute window into a single digest email to prevent notification fatigue
Scheduled notifications: send a birthday greeting or renewal reminder at a specific time per user's timezone
Delivery status tracking: queued, sent, delivered (provider ack), bounced, failed, opened, clicked per channel
In-app notification center: React inbox with unread count badge, mark-as-read, archive, and push-to-mobile fallback
Admin campaign builder: target a user segment (e.g. "all Pro plan users in EU"), preview audience size, schedule send, and track delivery metrics
Webhook and API: other services can trigger notifications via a REST API with a notification type and payload

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: At-least-once delivery semantics: every queued notification is attempted at least once; duplicates are silently deduplicated at the user level
Sub-5 second dispatch latency for in-app notifications (SignalR push)
Sub-60 second delivery latency for email and SMS from event trigger to provider send
10 million notifications per minute sustained throughput across all channels
Per-user deduplication window of 30 minutes: same notification type + entity ID within 30 min = suppress duplicate
Provider failover: if SendGrid returns 5xx, automatically retry on Amazon SES within 10 seconds
Horizontal scalability of the dispatch layer: 100x burst for a marketing campaign to 10M users
Delivery receipt processing: process 5M+ provider delivery callbacks per hour without data loss
GDPR compliance: users can export all their notification history and request full deletion

data.text: Build an ASP.NET Core application with a single NotificationService namespace. Templates are stored as JSON in SQL Server. A background IHostedService polls a NotificationQueue table every 5 seconds and dispatches emails via SendGrid SDK and SMS via Twilio SDK. In-app notifications are pushed via SignalR from the same process. This validates template rendering, preference filtering, and provider SDK integration.

data.title: Monolith Tech Stack
data.code:
Frontend:
  - React 18 with TypeScript
  - Vite for build tooling
  - Tailwind CSS for styling
  - React Query for server state
  - @microsoft/signalr for in-app real-time notification delivery

Backend (ASP.NET Core Monolith):
  - NotificationController: REST API for triggering notifications from other services
  - INotificationTemplateEngine: RazorLight / Scriban for template rendering with variables
  - Background NotificationWorker: polls NotificationQueue table every 5s, applies preference filter, dispatches
  - SendGrid SDK for email, Twilio SDK for SMS, FirebaseAdmin for FCM/APNs
  - SignalR for in-app push to online users
  - Polly policies: Retry (3x), CircuitBreaker (10 failures / 30s), Timeout (30s) per provider
  - SQL Server: NotificationTemplates, NotificationQueue, NotificationPreferences, NotificationDeliveryLog

Infrastructure:
  - Azure App Service or AWS ECS single-service deployment
  - Azure SQL or RDS: templates, queue, preferences, delivery log
  - Azure Cache for Redis: per-user preference cache, dedup window cache (SET with TTL)
  - Single process — throughput limited by single worker thread pool

data.text: Split the monolith into four microservices separated by concern. The Orchestrator Service evaluates preferences, deduplicates, and batches — it is the brain. The Provider Service handles the actual transport (SendGrid, Twilio, FCM) with circuit breakers and provider failover. The Preference Service manages per-user channel subscriptions, quiet hours, and category opt-ins. The Tracking Service ingests provider webhooks for delivery receipts and computes engagement metrics.

items: Orchestrator Service: The decision brain. Receives a trigger event (e.g. OrderShipped) via REST API or Kafka. Evaluates user preferences via Preference Service gRPC call. Applies the deduplication window check (Redis SET with TTL = 30 min keyed by userId:type:entityId). Applies quiet-hours rule based on user's timezone. Decides whether to send immediately, batch into a digest (using a 5-minute aggregation window), or suppress. Generates the final notification payload with rendered template variables and publishes a DispatchNotification command to the dispatch queue per channel.

Provider Service: The transport layer. Consumes DispatchNotification commands and routes to the correct provider: SendGrid for email (with template ID or raw HTML), Twilio for SMS, FCM for Android push, APNs for iOS push. Uses Polly for circuit-breaking: if SendGrid returns 5xx for 10 consecutive calls within 30 seconds, circuit opens and the notification is dead-lettered for manual or retry processing. Implements provider failover: email failures fall back to SES. Publishes ProviderSendResult events (success/failure with provider error code) consumed by Tracking Service.

Preference Service: Manages per-user notification preferences. Exposes a gRPC API: GetPreferences(userId) returns a NotificationPreferences proto (email: { orders: opt-in, marketing: opt-out, security: required }, push: { ... }, quietHours: { start: 22:00, end: 08:00, timezone: "America/New_York" }). Preferences are cached in Redis with 5-minute TTL and persisted in PostgreSQL. Exposes a React-admin-facing REST API for users to manage preferences.

Tracking Service: Ingests ProviderSendResult webhooks and SignalR delivery receipts. Stores per-notification delivery lifecycle in PostgreSQL: Queued → Sent → Delivered → Opened (email) / Clicked (email) / Failed. Computes channel-level delivery rate, open rate, and bounce rate. Exposes a REST API consumed by the admin analytics dashboard. Detects provider-level degradation (e.g., Twilio delivery rate drops below 90%) and emits a ProviderDegraded alert event.

Template Service: CRUD service for notification templates. Each template has: id, name, category (Order/Security/Marketing), channel, body template (Scriban/Liquid syntax), subject (email), variables schema, isActive, and A/B test variant config. Exposes a REST API consumed by the admin dashboard. On GET, renders the template with sample variables for live preview. Template versions are immutable — editing creates a new version; the active version is referenced by version ID.

Key Patterns:

  - PreferencesPanel saves with debounced React Query mutations and shows a 'saving' indicator

  - DeliveryMetrics uses Recharts with 10-second refresh for ops dashboards

data.title: Orchestrator Service — Preference Evaluation + Dedup + Dispatch

cards.title: In-App Push (Real-Time)
cards.description: Push in-app notifications to connected React clients via SignalR/WebSocket
pros: SignalR Service handles 1M+ concurrent connections with automatic scale-out
Connection groups enable efficient per-user push without broadcasting to all connections
cons: AWS AppSync requires a GraphQL schema even if only subscriptions are used

cards.title: Email Provider Integration
cards.description: Transactional and bulk email delivery with reputation management and bounce handling
tags: SendGrid (Azure Marketplace) / Azure Communication Services Email
pros: SES has the lowest per-email cost at scale (~$0.10/10k) with dedicated IP pools
SendGrid has the most flexible template engine and webhook event formats
cons: SES sandbox mode requires production access request; SendGrid free tier has daily caps

cards.title: SMS Provider Integration
cards.description: Transactional and promotional SMS with global reach and delivery receipts
pros: ACS supports opt-in management and compliance checklists out-of-the-box
SNS supports SMS spending limits per region to prevent cost overruns
cons: SNS does not support two-way SMS in all regions; ACS has broader two-way coverage

cards.title: Push Notifications (Mobile)
cards.description: APNs (iOS) and FCM (Android) push notification gateway with tag-based targeting
pros: Notification Hubs handles per-platform device registration and tag-based broadcast elegantly
SNS supports SMS, email, mobile push, and HTTP webhooks in a single service
cons: Notification Hubs does not support per-notification delivery receipt by default

cards.title: Message Queue
cards.description: Decouple event triggers from dispatch workers with priority lanes for critical vs marketing notifications
pros: Service Bus Premium supports sessions for ordered per-user delivery and duplicate detection
SQS FIFO + MessageGroupId enables ordered per-user processing with exactly-once deduplication
cons: SQS FIFO has a 300 TPS per queue limit that requires sharding for high-volume campaigns

cards.title: Database
cards.description: Persist notification history, preferences, templates, and delivery logs with strong consistency
tags: Azure SQL Database / Cosmos DB PostgreSQL
pros: Azure SQL with temporal tables enables point-in-time audit of preference changes
Aurora Serverless v2 auto-scales for bulk campaign write spikes
cons: Aurora cluster storage scaling can lag behind sudden 10M-row write spikes

data.title: When to Choose Microservices?
data.text: Start with a monolith. Split into microservices only when you have clear scaling bottlenecks, independent deployment needs, or team boundaries that justify the operational overhead.

data.title: Summary
points: At-least-once delivery + idempotency keys are the correct reliability primitive — never promise exactly-once across external providers
Per-user deduplication via Redis SET with TTL is simpler and more reliable than a distributed lock
Quiet hours require timezone-aware scheduling — never use UTC wall-clock for user-facing suppression
Provider failover (SendGrid → SES) must be transparent to the caller — the Provider Service owns retry logic
The MassTransit outbox pattern guarantees DispatchNotification durability without two-phase commit
Digest mode (5-min aggregation window) requires the Orchestrator to hold state in Redis sorted sets per user until the window closes
data.takeaway: Notification systems succeed on reliability and user experience, not raw throughput. Preference-aware dispatch with Redis dedup windows, an outbox-backed Orchestrator for crash safety, provider failover with circuit breakers, and timezone-aware quiet hours are the architectural decisions that keep users informed without spamming them.
